stem: An elderly patient falls onto an outstretched hand. Radiographs show a distal radius fracture with **dorsal angulation** of the distal fragment ("dinner-fork" deformity). What is the eponym?

images.caption: Colles fracture — dorsal angulation
images.alt: Lateral wrist radiograph schematic showing dorsal angulation of the distal radius

explanation: A **Colles fracture** is an extra-articular distal radius fracture with **dorsal** displacement/angulation, typically from a FOOSH in osteoporotic bone. A **Smith** fracture is the reverse (volar angulation). A **Barton** fracture is an intra-articular rim fracture with carpal subluxation; a **Galeazzi** injury is a radial shaft fracture with distal radioulnar joint disruption.
references: Rockwood & Green's Fractures in Adults — Distal Radius

stem: A young man has wrist pain and **anatomic snuffbox tenderness** after a fall, but initial radiographs are normal. Which statement about the likely fracture is correct?

options.text: The scaphoid is involved; the proximal pole is at risk of avascular necrosis
The lunate is involved; it never develops avascular necrosis
The triquetrum is involved; it is the most commonly fractured carpal bone
No fracture is possible if initial X-rays are normal

explanation: Snuffbox tenderness signals a **scaphoid fracture** — the most commonly fractured carpal bone. Its blood supply enters **distally and runs retrograde**, so **proximal pole** fractures risk **avascular necrosis** and non-union. Initial films are often normal: immobilize and re-image (or obtain MRI/CT) rather than clear the patient. (Avascular necrosis of the **lunate** is Kienböck disease.)
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Carpal Fractures
